als.title: ALS — if, when and whenever
als.goal: Choose als in a real situation and put finite verbs in the correct clauses without first translating word-for-word from English.
als.overview: ALS is a subordinating conjunction (onderschikkend voegwoord). It introduces a subordinate clause (bijzin) for a condition (if), a future time (when), or a habitual event (whenever). The rest of the sentence still follows main-clause V2.
als.status: Detailed lesson, AI-edited. The toen / als / wanneer and the wanneer register statements were checked against two Taaladvies.net pages on 26 October 2026; the rest is not independently reviewed and there is no native-speaker certification.

formulas.label: Main clause then subordinate clause
formulas.pattern: Ik bel je | als ik thuis ben.
formulas.why: The finite verb bel follows ik in the main clause; ben closes the simple subordinate clause.

formulas.label: Subordinate clause first
formulas.pattern: Als ik thuis ben, | bel ik je.
formulas.why: The whole als-clause fills position one. Bel therefore precedes subject ik in the main clause (inversion).

formulas.label: Multiple verbs
formulas.pattern: Als ik het verslag heb afgemaakt, | stuur ik het op.
formulas.why: A subordinate clause can finish with a verb cluster (heb afgemaakt). Don't insist that the finite verb always be the single last word.

sections.title: 1. What does ALS mean?
sections.body: ALS covers a condition (if), a future time (when) and repeated situations (whenever). Meaning comes from the situation, not from a word-by-word rule.

examples.nl: Als ik tijd heb, help ik je.
examples.en: If I have time, I will help you.

examples.nl: Ik bel je als ik thuis ben.
examples.en: I will call you when I am home.

examples.nl: Als ik moe ben, drink ik vaak thee.
examples.en: Whenever I am tired, I often drink tea.

sections.title: 2. What changes inside the subordinate clause?
sections.body: Compare ik ben thuis with als ik thuis ben. In a one-verb subordinate clause the finite verb normally follows the other elements. With multi-verb constructions, the final verb cluster has its own ordering rules.

examples.nl: Ik ben klaar.
examples.en: I am ready.

examples.nl: Als ik klaar ben, bel ik je.
examples.en: When I am ready, I will call you.

examples.nl: Als ik het werk kan afmaken, stuur ik je een bericht.
examples.en: If I can finish the work, I will send you a message.

sections.title: 3. Why does inversion happen?
sections.body: When the complete als-clause comes first, that entire clause is one constituent occupying position one. Dutch main-clause V2 puts the conjugated main verb immediately afterwards, before its subject.

examples.nl: Ik help je als ik klaar ben.
examples.en: I will help you when I am ready.

examples.nl: Als ik klaar ben, help ik je.
examples.en: When I am ready, I will help you.

examples.nl: Als de test slaagt, starten we de applicatie.
examples.en: If the test succeeds, we start the application.

sections.title: 4. Future conditions and recurring situations in the past
sections.body: Future contexts normally use a present-tense verb inside the als-clause. A repeated past habit uses als (or the more formal wanneer) with a past tense, often with 'telkens' or 'vroeger'. A single particular past occasion uses toen. In Belgium, als or wanneer for one single past event is not standard: toen is the correct conjunction there.

examples.nl: Als je morgen komt, maken we eten.
examples.en: When you come tomorrow, we will cook.

examples.nl: Als ik vroeger vrij was, ging ik fietsen.
examples.en: Whenever I was free in the past, I went cycling.

examples.nl: Toen ik gisteren thuiskwam, was ik moe.
examples.en: When I got home yesterday, I was tired.

sections.title: 5. Als vs wanneer vs toen
sections.body: Als and wanneer can both express a moment in time or a condition, and in practice they are usually interchangeable with the present or future. Wanneer is the more formal, written choice; als is the neutral one. Context can tip the reading: 'als' is easily heard as 'if', 'wanneer' as 'when'. In a direct question wanneer is the question word; in an indirect question it introduces subordinate order. Toen refers to one specific past occasion or period.

examples.nl: Wanneer begint de vergadering?
examples.en: When does the meeting start?

examples.nl: Ik weet niet wanneer de vergadering begint.
examples.en: I don't know when the meeting begins.

examples.nl: Toen ik aankwam, was de winkel dicht.
examples.en: When I arrived, the shop was closed.

sections.title: 6. Modal verbs, perfect tense and verb clusters
sections.body: Dutch subordinate clauses often contain a group of verbs near the end. The internal order can vary with the construction and sometimes by regional preference. Learn common natural clusters rather than forcing a universal finite-verb-last formula.

examples.nl: Als ik kan komen, bel ik je.
examples.en: If I can come, I will call you.

examples.nl: Als ik het verslag heb geschreven, stuur ik het door.
examples.en: When I have written the report, I forward it.

examples.nl: Ik kom langs als ik de fout kan herstellen.
examples.en: I will come by if I can fix the error.

sections.title: 7. Separable verbs inside an als-clause
sections.body: In ordinary main clauses a finite separable verb splits (de server valt uit); in a simple subordinate clause, the finite form rejoins (als de server uitvalt). The main clause after a fronted subordinate clause still requires inversion.

examples.nl: De server valt uit.
examples.en: The server goes down.

examples.nl: Als de server uitvalt, controleer ik de logs.
examples.en: If the server goes down, I check the logs.

examples.nl: Als ik het formulier invul, controleer ik mijn gegevens.
examples.en: When I fill in the form, I check my details.

sections.title: 8. Recognise meaning rather than relying on hints
sections.body: A reason uses omdat, a one-time past event often uses toen, a condition or repeated occasion often uses als. In independent practice, decide which construction is appropriate before seeing the model sentence.

examples.nl: Ik blijf thuis omdat ik ziek ben.
examples.en: I stay home because I am sick.

examples.nl: Als ik ziek ben, blijf ik thuis.
examples.en: If I am sick, I stay home.

examples.nl: Toen ik ziek was, bleef ik thuis.
examples.en: When I was sick, I stayed home.

sections.title: 9. Als with dan, and pas als
sections.body: After a fronted als-clause Dutch often adds 'dan' (then) to pick the condition up again. It changes nothing about the order: the finite verb still follows immediately, so you hear 'dan blijf ik', never 'dan ik blijf'. With 'pas als' (only when, not until) the same holds: the whole clause counts as position one and the main verb comes next.

examples.nl: Als het regent, dan blijf ik thuis.
examples.en: If it rains, then I stay at home.

examples.nl: Als je vragen hebt, bel me dan.
examples.en: If you have questions, call me then.

examples.nl: Pas als de toegang werkt, beginnen we met de controle.
examples.en: Only when access works do we start the check.

sections.title: 10. Negation, 'er' and the verb group inside an als-clause
sections.body: 'Niet' normally stands in front of the final verb or verb group of the als-clause, and 'geen' replaces 'niet een' before a noun without article. When the subject is indefinite ('a warning', 'unsaved work'), Dutch often places 'er' directly after als; the real subject follows and the finite verb closes the clause.

examples.nl: Als ik niet kan slapen, lees ik een boek.
examples.en: When I can't sleep, I read a book.

examples.nl: Als je de weg niet weet, vraag het aan iemand.
examples.en: If you don't know the way, ask someone.

examples.nl: Stop de test als er een onverwachte waarschuwing verschijnt.
examples.en: Stop the test if an unexpected warning appears.

sections.title: 11. Not every 'als' opens a clause
sections.body: The conjunction als is followed by its own subject and finite verb. When only a noun or pronoun follows, als means 'as' or 'like' (a role or a comparison) and the verb-final order does not apply, because there is no clause. Check for a subject plus a conjugated verb before you apply the rule.

examples.nl: Ik werk als systeembeheerder.
examples.en: I work as a system administrator.

examples.nl: Dat klinkt als een goed plan.
examples.en: That sounds like a good plan.

examples.nl: Mijn zus is net zo lang als ik.
examples.en: My sister is just as tall as I am.

mistakes.wrong: Als ik ben moe, blijf ik thuis.
mistakes.right: Als ik moe ben, blijf ik thuis.
mistakes.why: Ben follows moe in this simple subordinate clause.

mistakes.wrong: Als het klaar is, ik stuur het.
mistakes.right: Als het klaar is, stuur ik het.
mistakes.why: The fronted als-clause is position one: the following finite verb precedes subject ik.

mistakes.wrong: Als ik gisteren aankwam, belde ik haar.
mistakes.right: Toen ik gisteren aankwam, belde ik haar.
mistakes.why: A single, specific completed past arrival normally uses toen; als is natural for repeated past or hypothetical contexts.

mistakes.wrong: Als het regent, dan ik blijf thuis.
mistakes.right: Als het regent, dan blijf ik thuis.
mistakes.why: Even with 'dan', the finite verb comes directly after it and before the subject: 'dan blijf ik'.

mistakes.wrong: Ik werk als ik systeembeheerder ben, elke dag.
mistakes.right: Ik werk als systeembeheerder.
mistakes.why: Here als means 'as' (a role), not a conjunction; adding a clause 'als ik ... ben' changes the meaning to a condition.

Wanneer of als en tegenwoordige of toekomende tijd — Taaladvies.net

separable.title: Separable verbs — scheidbare werkwoorden
separable.goal: Choose correctly among stuur ... op, opsturen, opgestuurd, opstuurt and op te sturen, understand why, and tell separable verbs from inseparable lookalikes.
separable.overview: A separable verb is a particle plus a verb (op + sturen). The particle carries the stress and moves: it stays behind in a main clause where the verb takes position two, and it is written together with the verb everywhere else (infinitive, participle, dependent clause). Verbs with an unstressed prefix such as be-, ver-, ont- or her- are inseparable and never split.
separable.status: Detailed lesson, AI-edited and aligned with the separable-verb forms table (68 verbs). The forms are authored but not yet checked by a native speaker; no external source has been checked for the stress-dependent verbs, so those are qualified.

formulas.label: Present main clause
formulas.pattern: Ik stuur het verslag op.
formulas.why: Stuur is the finite V2 verb and op comes later.

formulas.label: Simple past
formulas.pattern: Ik stuurde het verslag op.
formulas.why: The particle remains separate in this finite main clause.

formulas.label: Perfect tense
formulas.pattern: Ik heb het verslag opgestuurd.
formulas.why: For opsturen, the participle is op + ge + stuurd; the auxiliary is heb.

formulas.label: Modal + infinitive
formulas.pattern: Ik moet het verslag opsturen.
formulas.why: The infinitive opsturen remains joined.

formulas.label: Subordinate clause
formulas.pattern: Ik weet dat hij het verslag opstuurt.
formulas.why: The single finite form appears joined at the end of the subordinate clause.

formulas.label: Te-infinitive
formulas.pattern: Ik probeer het verslag op te sturen.
formulas.why: Te goes between the particle and the verb.

formulas.label: Where the particle goes (main clause)
formulas.pattern: Ik | stuur | het verslag | op.
formulas.why: Slot two holds the finite verb stuur; the particle op waits at the end of the clause, behind every object and adverbial.

formulas.label: Where the particle goes (joined forms)
formulas.pattern: opsturen | opgestuurd | op te sturen | dat ik opstuur
formulas.why: Whenever the verb is not finite in slot two, the particle stays attached: infinitive, participle with ge- inside, te between particle and verb, and the finite form at the end of a dependent clause.

formulas.label: Imperative
formulas.pattern: Stuur | het verslag | op!
formulas.why: The imperative is a main clause: the stem comes first and the particle is split off to the end.

sections.title: 1. Why do separable verbs split?
sections.body: A main clause needs its finite verb in position two. In a separable verb the finite part is the stem (stuur) and the particle (op) is left behind and goes to the end of the clause. The particle is stressed and carries part of the meaning: 'opsturen' means to send off, 'sturen' only to send. Read the end of a Dutch main clause carefully, because the particle that completes the verb may be the last word.

examples.nl: Ik stuur het verslag op.
examples.en: I send off the report.

examples.nl: Ik bel mijn collega terug.
examples.en: I call my colleague back.

examples.nl: Ik schakel de testserver uit.
examples.en: I switch off the test server.

sections.title: 2. Watch the particle move
sections.body: Compare one verb in six places. Main clause: 'Ik stuur het verslag op'. Past: 'Ik stuurde het verslag op'. Modal: 'Ik moet het verslag opsturen'. Perfect: 'Ik heb het verslag opgestuurd'. Dependent clause: 'dat hij het verslag opstuurt'. With te: 'Ik probeer het verslag op te sturen'. The particle is detached only in the first two, where the verb itself sits in position two.

examples.nl: Ik moet het verslag opsturen.
examples.en: I have to send off the report.

examples.nl: Ik weet dat hij het verslag opstuurt.
examples.en: I know that he sends off the report.

examples.nl: Ik probeer het verslag op te sturen.
examples.en: I try to send off the report.

sections.title: 3. The participle: ge- goes inside
sections.body: For a separable verb the participle is particle + ge + stem: op + ge + stuurd, terug + ge + beld, uit + ge + schakeld. Regular stems end in -d or -t as usual, and strong verbs keep their strong participle: opgenomen, deelgenomen, afgesproken. Verbs whose stem starts with an unstressed prefix get no ge-: voorbereid, not voorgebereid. Verbs of movement or change of state take zijn (aangekomen, opgestaan, uitgevallen), most others hebben.

examples.nl: Ik heb het verslag opgestuurd.
examples.en: I have sent off the report.

examples.nl: Ik ben op kantoor aangekomen.
examples.en: I have arrived at the office.

examples.nl: Ik heb de presentatie voorbereid.
examples.en: I have prepared the presentation.

sections.title: 4. Te goes between particle and verb
sections.body: The te-infinitive is written in three parts: particle, te, verb. 'op te sturen', 'in te leveren', 'mee te brengen'. After a modal there is no te and the infinitive is whole: 'moet opsturen'. The three-part group stays together at the end of its clause.

examples.nl: Ik probeer mijn werk op tijd in te leveren.
examples.en: I try to hand in my work on time.

examples.nl: Ik besluit het antwoord af te wachten.
examples.en: I decide to wait for the answer.

examples.nl: Ik moet om zeven uur opstaan.
examples.en: I have to get up at seven.

sections.title: 5. Dependent clauses and the imperative
sections.body: In a dependent clause the finite verb goes to the end and is written together with its particle: 'dat hij het verslag opstuurt'. The imperative is a main clause, so it splits again: 'Stuur het verslag op!'. This is why the same verb can look different in two clauses of one sentence.

examples.nl: Ik weet dat zij het adres opschrijft.
examples.en: I know that she writes down the address.

examples.nl: Stuur het verslag op!
examples.en: Send off the report!

examples.nl: Ik zie dat de klant binnenkomt.
examples.en: I see that the customer is coming in.

sections.title: 6. Reflexive verbs and fixed prepositions
sections.body: Some separable verbs are reflexive: 'zich aanmelden', 'zich inschrijven', 'zich uitschrijven'. The reflexive pronoun stays near the verb: 'Ik meld me aan'. Some take a fixed preposition: 'deelnemen aan', 'meedoen aan', 'aanmelden voor'. The preposition belongs to the verb and does not replace the particle.

examples.nl: Ik meld me aan voor de cursus.
examples.en: I register for the course.

examples.nl: Ik neem deel aan de vergadering.
examples.en: I take part in the meeting.

examples.nl: Ik doe mee aan de cursus.
examples.en: I join the course.

sections.title: 7. Inseparable verbs: do not split them
sections.body: Verbs that begin with an unstressed prefix such as be-, ge-, ver-, ont- and her- are inseparable. The stress falls on the stem, they never split, and their participle has no ge-: bezoeken (bezocht), begrijpen (begrepen), ontdekken (ontdekt), verkopen (verkocht), overwegen (overwogen). A verb that merely starts with a letter group is not automatically separable, so learn each verb with its stress.

examples.nl: Ik bezoek mijn collega.
examples.en: I visit my colleague.

examples.nl: Ik begrijp het probleem.
examples.en: I understand the problem.

examples.nl: Ik heb de fout ontdekt.
examples.en: I have discovered the error.

sections.title: 8. Lookalikes that depend on stress and meaning
sections.body: A few verbs exist in both forms with different meanings. 'Voorkomen' with stress on the stem means to prevent and is inseparable ('Ik voorkom het probleem'); with stress on the particle it means to occur and is separable ('Dat komt vaak voor'). Treat such pairs as two different verbs and check the meaning before you decide whether to split.

examples.nl: Ik voorkom het probleem.
examples.en: I prevent the problem.

examples.nl: Dat komt vaak voor.
examples.en: That happens often.

examples.nl: Ik heb het probleem voorkomen.
examples.en: I have prevented the problem.

sections.title: 9. Combining the rules
sections.body: Real sentences combine several rules. After a fronted dependent clause the main clause inverts and the particle still goes to the end: 'Als het systeem uitvalt, schakel ik de server uit'. In the past with a time word first: 'Gisteren sloot ik de sessie af'. In the perfect the particle disappears into the participle: 'Ik heb de sessie afgesloten'. Ask three questions in order: which verb is finite, which position does it sit in, and is it the finite verb or a form of the verb that carries the particle?

examples.nl: Als het systeem uitvalt, schakel ik de server uit.
examples.en: If the system fails, I switch off the server.

examples.nl: Gisteren sloot ik de sessie af.
examples.en: Yesterday I ended the session.

examples.nl: Ik heb de sessie afgesloten.
examples.en: I have ended the session.

mistakes.wrong: Ik opstuur het verslag.
mistakes.right: Ik stuur het verslag op.
mistakes.why: Finite main-clause separable verbs split.

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb het verslag gestuurd op.
mistakes.right: Ik heb het verslag opgestuurd.
mistakes.why: The past participle of opsturen is the joined form opgestuurd: op + ge + stuurd. You do not leave op behind the participle.

mistakes.wrong: Ik probeer te opsturen het verslag.
mistakes.right: Ik probeer het verslag op te sturen.
mistakes.why: Te separates the particle from the infinitive.

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb het verslag voorgebereid.
mistakes.right: Ik heb het verslag voorbereid.
mistakes.why: Voorbereiden contains the unstressed prefix be-, so the participle takes no ge-: voorbereid.

mistakes.wrong: Ik begrijp het probleem niet te.
mistakes.right: Ik begrijp het probleem niet.
mistakes.why: Begrijpen is inseparable and has no particle, so nothing is left to put at the end; the verb never splits.

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb op kantoor aangekomen.
mistakes.right: Ik ben op kantoor aangekomen.
mistakes.why: Aankomen is a verb of movement and forms its perfect with zijn, so the auxiliary is ben.

inversion.title: Verb second & inversion — de persoonsvorm op plaats twee
inversion.goal: Build Dutch statements without translating English word order: identify the first whole phrase, put the conjugated verb second, then place the subject.
inversion.overview: In an ordinary Dutch statement, the finite verb (persoonsvorm) is the second sentence constituent—not necessarily the second word. If a time phrase, place phrase or entire subordinate clause comes first, the subject usually follows the finite verb. This is inversion (inversie).
inversion.status: Expanded teaching module (AI-edited, not independently reviewed by a native speaker); broader course and exercise review pending.

formulas.label: Subject first
formulas.pattern: Ik | werk | vandaag thuis.
formulas.why: Ik is the first constituent; werk is the finite verb in position two.

formulas.label: Time first — inversion
formulas.pattern: Vandaag | werk | ik thuis.
formulas.why: Vandaag takes the first position, so werk follows before subject ik.

formulas.label: Subordinate clause first — inversion
formulas.pattern: Als ik thuis ben, | bel | ik je.
formulas.why: The whole als-clause is one first constituent. Bel is therefore in the second position of the main clause; ik comes after it.

formulas.label: Modal and perfect forms
formulas.pattern: Morgen | moet | ik werken. / Gisteren | heb | ik gewerkt.
formulas.why: Only the conjugated part (moet/heb) occupies V2. The infinitive or participle usually stays later.

sections.title: 1. Why does Dutch invert the subject?
sections.body: English normally keeps 'I work' after today; Dutch treats Vandaag as the first sentence constituent and puts the finite verb directly after it. A constituent can contain several words: Na het werk is still just one opening phrase.

examples.nl: Ik ga na het werk naar huis.
examples.en: I go home after work.

examples.nl: Na het werk ga ik naar huis.
examples.en: After work I go home.

examples.nl: Om negen uur begint de vergadering.
examples.en: The meeting starts at nine o'clock.

sections.title: 2. What counts as position one?
sections.body: Count phrases, not individual words. A place phrase, object or entire subordinate clause can occupy position one. Find the finite verb first; then identify the subject.

examples.nl: Op tafel ligt een boek.
examples.en: There is a book lying on the table.

examples.nl: Dat boek heb ik al gelezen.
examples.en: I've already read that book.

examples.nl: Als ik tijd heb, help ik je.
examples.en: If I have time, I'll help you.

sections.title: 3. One conjugated verb; other verbs stay elsewhere
sections.body: With a modal, perfect tense or a separable verb, the finite verb still goes into position two. A non-finite verb or separable particle belongs later in the main clause.

examples.nl: Morgen moet ik vroeg opstaan.
examples.en: Tomorrow I have to get up early.

examples.nl: Gisteren heb ik de printer gerepareerd.
examples.en: Yesterday I repaired the printer.

examples.nl: Na het werk ruim ik de keuken op.
examples.en: After work I tidy the kitchen.

sections.title: 4. Why do questions look different?
sections.body: The V2 rule discussed here applies to ordinary statements. Yes/no questions often begin with the finite verb; commands can begin with an imperative. Don't mechanically force every Dutch sentence into subject-first V2.

examples.nl: Werk je vandaag thuis?
examples.en: Are you working from home today?

examples.nl: Wanneer begint de vergadering?
examples.en: When does the meeting start?

examples.nl: Kom morgen terug!
examples.en: Come back tomorrow!

sections.title: 5. Say it without translating
sections.body: Choose your opening first (Vandaag, Na het werk, Als ik klaar ben), locate the conjugated verb, then say the subject. A common mistake is translating 'Today I work' as Vandaag ik werk.

examples.nl: Vandaag leer ik Nederlands.
examples.en: Today I am learning Dutch.

examples.nl: Als de printer klaar is, haal ik het document op.
examples.en: When the printer is finished, I collect the document.

examples.nl: Daarom bel ik je later.
examples.en: That's why I'll call you later.

mistakes.wrong: Vandaag ik werk thuis.
mistakes.right: Vandaag werk ik thuis.
mistakes.why: Vandaag takes position one and finite werk must immediately follow it; ik moves behind werk.

mistakes.wrong: Als ik klaar ben, ik bel je.
mistakes.right: Als ik klaar ben, bel ik je.
mistakes.why: The fronted subordinate clause counts as position one of the main clause, so bel comes before subject ik.

mistakes.wrong: Morgen ik moet vroeg opstaan.
mistakes.right: Morgen moet ik vroeg opstaan.
mistakes.why: Morgen is first; modal verb moet is finite and takes V2, while infinitive opstaan stays later.

sources: Sentence structure: main and subordinate clause word order — UCL

omdat.title: Omdat — giving a reason
omdat.goal: Explain why something happens, place the verb group correctly, and choose between omdat, want and daarom.
omdat.overview: Omdat means 'because' and introduces a subordinate clause (bijzin). The verb or verb cluster normally occurs toward the end of that clause. But want connects two main clauses, and daarom ('therefore') is an adverb in a main clause.
omdat.status: Expanded teaching module (AI-edited, not independently reviewed by a native speaker); broader course and exercise review pending.

formulas.label: Reason comes second
formulas.pattern: Ik blijf thuis | omdat ik ziek ben.
formulas.why: Blijf is the finite main-clause verb; ben moves to the end of the simple omdat-clause.

formulas.label: Reason comes first
formulas.pattern: Omdat ik ziek ben, | blijf ik thuis.
formulas.why: The whole reason-clause occupies position one, so the main-clause verb blijf comes before ik.

formulas.label: Compare WANT and DAAROM
formulas.pattern: Ik blijf thuis, want ik ben ziek. / Ik ben ziek. Daarom blijf ik thuis.
formulas.why: Want connects a main clause with another main clause (ik ben ziek); daarom begins a main clause and triggers V2 inversion.

sections.title: 1. What question does omdat answer?
sections.body: Use omdat to answer waarom (why?). It gives the reason for a fact, decision or action. Translate the relationship, not English word order.

examples.nl: Ik leer Nederlands omdat ik in België woon.
examples.en: I am learning Dutch because I live in Belgium.

examples.nl: De vergadering begint later omdat de trein vertraging heeft.
examples.en: The meeting starts later because the train is delayed.

examples.nl: Ik bel de helpdesk omdat mijn computer niet werkt.
examples.en: I'm calling the help desk because my computer isn't working.

sections.title: 2. Why does the verb move?
sections.body: Omdat introduces a subordinate clause. Compare the independent statement 'Ik ben ziek' with 'omdat ik ziek ben'. With multiple verbs, a verb cluster forms toward the end; don't claim the finite verb is always the absolute final word.

examples.nl: Ik ben ziek.
examples.en: I am ill.

examples.nl: Ik blijf thuis omdat ik ziek ben.
examples.en: I stay home because I am ill.

examples.nl: Ik blijf thuis omdat ik morgen moet werken.
examples.en: I stay home because I have to work tomorrow.

sections.title: 3. Reason first → inversion in the main clause
sections.body: If you begin with the entire omdat-clause, it fills the first position of the main clause. The main finite verb must come directly afterward, before its subject.

examples.nl: Omdat het regent, neem ik de bus.
examples.en: Because it's raining, I'm taking the bus.

examples.nl: Omdat de server niet reageert, controleer ik de logs.
examples.en: Because the server isn't responding, I check the logs.

examples.nl: Omdat ik geen tijd heb, kom ik morgen terug.
examples.en: Because I don't have time, I'll come back tomorrow.

sections.title: 4. Omdat versus want versus daarom
sections.body: Omdat begins a subordinate reason clause. Want joins main clauses without moving the second clause's finite verb to the end. Daarom states a result and must respect main-clause V2. These aren't interchangeable word for word.

examples.nl: Ik ga naar huis omdat ik moe ben.
examples.en: I'm going home because I'm tired.

examples.nl: Ik ga naar huis, want ik ben moe.
examples.en: I'm going home, because I'm tired.

examples.nl: Ik ben moe. Daarom ga ik naar huis.
examples.en: I'm tired. That's why I'm going home.

sections.title: 5. Don't confuse a reason with a condition
sections.body: Omdat means the reason is presented as true. Als expresses a condition or recurring time: the second sentence does not assert that you're ill right now.

examples.nl: Ik blijf thuis omdat ik ziek ben.
examples.en: I'm staying home because I'm ill.

examples.nl: Als ik ziek ben, blijf ik thuis.
examples.en: If I'm ill, I stay home.

examples.nl: Als de test mislukt, stoppen we.
examples.en: If the test fails, we'll stop.

mistakes.wrong: Ik blijf thuis omdat ik ben ziek.
mistakes.right: Ik blijf thuis omdat ik ziek ben.
mistakes.why: In this simple subordinate clause, predicate ziek comes before finite ben.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat het regent, ik neem de bus.
mistakes.right: Omdat het regent, neem ik de bus.
mistakes.why: The complete omdat-clause fills the first main-clause position; finite neem therefore precedes ik.

mistakes.wrong: Ik ben moe, daarom ik ga naar huis.
mistakes.right: Ik ben moe, daarom ga ik naar huis.
mistakes.why: Daarom is the first element of its main clause, so V2 requires ga ik.

sources: Omdat at the beginning of a sentence — Team Taaladvies Vlaanderen
Omdat and doordat — Team Taaladvies Vlaanderen

dat.title: Dat — reporting what someone thinks or says
dat.goal: Use dat for embedded statements, distinguish it from 'that' as a demonstrative or relative pronoun, and put verbs correctly.
dat.overview: After verbs such as denken, zeggen, weten and hopen, dat often introduces what a person thinks, says or knows. This subordinate clause places its verb group toward the end. The word dat also has other functions, so recognise the sentence structure.
dat.status: Expanded teaching module (AI-edited, not independently reviewed by a native speaker); broader course and exercise review pending.

formulas.label: Report an idea
formulas.pattern: Ik denk | dat hij morgen komt.
formulas.why: The main clause has finite denk; the subordinate statement has finite komt at the end.

formulas.label: Verb group in a reported statement
formulas.pattern: Ze zegt | dat ze morgen moet werken.
formulas.why: Moet werken forms a final verb group in the dat-clause.

formulas.label: Another DAT (demonstrative)
formulas.pattern: Dat boek is van mij.
formulas.why: Here dat points to a het-word noun ('that book'); it does not introduce a reported clause.

sections.title: 1. Why use dat after denken or zeggen?
sections.body: One clause introduces the speaker's thought or report, and the dat-clause says what the thought or message is. English may omit 'that', but Dutch often includes dat, especially in clear reported statements.

examples.nl: Ik denk dat hij thuis is.
examples.en: I think that he is at home.

examples.nl: Ze zegt dat de printer kapot is.
examples.en: She says that the printer is broken.

examples.nl: Ik hoop dat je morgen komt.
examples.en: I hope you come tomorrow.

sections.title: 2. Main clause versus subordinate clause
sections.body: Compare 'Hij komt morgen' with 'dat hij morgen komt'. In a basic dat-clause the finite verb moves behind most other elements. With modals and perfect tenses the final group can contain several verbs.

examples.nl: Hij komt morgen.
examples.en: He is coming tomorrow.

examples.nl: Ik weet dat hij morgen komt.
examples.en: I know that he is coming tomorrow.

examples.nl: Ik denk dat hij de fout kan oplossen.
examples.en: I think he can fix the error.

sections.title: 3. Dat with perfect tense and separable verbs
sections.body: The subordinate clause can end in a verb cluster. With a simple finite separable verb, the prefix rejoins the verb in the dat-clause.

examples.nl: Ik weet dat ze het verslag heeft verstuurd.
examples.en: I know that she has sent the report.

examples.nl: Ze zegt dat de server uitvalt.
examples.en: She says that the server is going down.

examples.nl: Ik denk dat hij het formulier heeft ingevuld.
examples.en: I think that he has filled in the form.

sections.title: 4. DAT is not always a conjunction
sections.body: Dat can mean 'that' before a het-word (demonstrative), or introduce a relative clause after a het-word. Do not tag every occurrence of the letters dat as a reported statement.

examples.nl: Dat document ligt op de printer.
examples.en: That document is lying on the printer.

examples.nl: Het document dat ik lees, is interessant.
examples.en: The document that I'm reading is interesting.

examples.nl: Ik denk dat het document klaar is.
examples.en: I think the document is ready.

sections.title: 5. Report without translating word by word
sections.body: Before answering, decide whether you're making your own statement or reporting someone's knowledge. For a report: main clause + dat + subordinate clause; keep the finite verb in the correct group.

examples.nl: Ik weet dat je vandaag werkt.
examples.en: I know you're working today.

examples.nl: Mijn collega zegt dat hij later belt.
examples.en: My colleague says he'll call later.

examples.nl: Ik geloof dat we genoeg tijd hebben.
examples.en: I believe we have enough time.

mistakes.wrong: Ik denk dat hij komt morgen.
mistakes.right: Ik denk dat hij morgen komt.
mistakes.why: In the basic reported dat-clause, morgen comes before finite komt.

mistakes.wrong: Ze zegt dat ze moet morgen werken.
mistakes.right: Ze zegt dat ze morgen moet werken.
mistakes.why: A modal verb group usually closes this subordinate clause: morgen comes before moet werken.

mistakes.wrong: Ik weet dat hij is ziek.
mistakes.right: Ik weet dat hij ziek is.
mistakes.why: The simple subordinate clause places predicate ziek before finite is.

sources: Subordinate clauses including dat — UCL Dutch grammar

toen.title: TOEN — one occasion or period in the past
toen.goal: Use toen for a single past occasion or a closed period, put the verb last in the toen-clause, and tell it apart from toen meaning 'then', and from als and wanneer.
toen.overview: As a conjunction, toen opens a dependent clause about one specific moment or one closed period in the past. It is never used for the present or the future. Like every dependent clause it puts the finite verb at the end, and when the toen-clause comes first the main clause inverts. Toen is also an ordinary adverb meaning 'then', and that use is a main clause with the verb second.
toen.status: Detailed lesson, AI-edited. The statements on single occasion versus repeated occasion, on als and wanneer for repetition, and on Belgian usage were checked against Taaladvies pages on 27 October 2026 (see sources). Everything else is not independently reviewed by a native speaker.

formulas.label: Toen-clause first
formulas.pattern: Toen ik thuiskwam, | belde ik Zoë.
formulas.why: The whole toen-clause fills position one, so the main clause starts with the finite verb belde and the subject ik follows it.

formulas.label: Main clause first
formulas.pattern: Ik zag haar | toen ik de straat overstak.
formulas.why: The main clause keeps normal order, and the toen-clause ends with overstak.

formulas.label: Toen as an adverb
formulas.pattern: Toen | belde | ik mijn collega.
formulas.why: Here toen means 'then', fills position one on its own, and the verb belde stays second. There is no dependent clause.

formulas.label: Earlier action
formulas.pattern: Toen ik aankwam, | was de vergadering al begonnen.
formulas.why: The past perfect in the main clause (was ... begonnen) shows that the meeting started before the arrival.

sections.title: 1. What does toen mean?
sections.body: Toen as a conjunction refers to one particular moment or one closed period in the past: the evening you arrived, the years you lived in Amsterdam. It answers 'when exactly?' for something that happened, and it does not work for the present or the future. The question is always whether you can point to that one occasion or period.

examples.nl: Toen ik thuiskwam, belde ik Zoë.
examples.en: When I got home, I called Zoë.

examples.nl: Toen ik in Amsterdam woonde, werkte ik bij een bank.
examples.en: When I lived in Amsterdam, I worked at a bank.

examples.nl: Toen de storing begon, belde ik de helpdesk.
examples.en: When the outage started, I called the helpdesk.

sections.title: 2. The verb goes last inside the toen-clause
sections.body: A toen-clause is a dependent clause: subject first, then the other elements, and the finite verb at the end. A separable verb is written together there, so thuiskomen becomes thuiskwam and aankomen becomes aankwam. In a main clause the same verb would split, as in 'Ik kwam thuis'.

examples.nl: Toen ik het bestand opende, verscheen er een foutmelding.
examples.en: When I opened the file, an error message appeared.

examples.nl: Toen het alarm afging, liep iedereen naar buiten.
examples.en: When the alarm went off, everyone walked outside.

examples.nl: Toen ik aankwam, was de winkel dicht.
examples.en: When I arrived, the shop was closed.

sections.title: 3. Toen-clause first or main clause first
sections.body: If the toen-clause opens the sentence, it is one first constituent, so the main clause starts with its finite verb and the subject follows (inversion). If the main clause comes first, nothing changes in it, and the toen-clause closes the sentence. Both orders say the same thing; the first stresses the moment, the second the event.

examples.nl: Toen de lift stopte, zaten we vast.
examples.en: When the lift stopped, we were stuck.

examples.nl: De server crashte toen wij de update installeerden.
examples.en: The server crashed when we installed the update.

examples.nl: Ik schrok toen de telefoon midden in de nacht ging.
examples.en: I was startled when the phone rang in the middle of the night.

sections.title: 4. Toen as 'then' is a different word
sections.body: Toen is also an adverb meaning 'then' or 'at that point' in a story. As an adverb it fills position one alone, so the verb stays second and the subject follows it, and there is no comma and no second clause. The test is simple: if the verb goes to the end, toen is a conjunction; if the verb is second, toen is an adverb.

examples.nl: Toen belde ik mijn collega.
examples.en: Then I called my colleague.

examples.nl: Toen ging het licht uit.
examples.en: Then the light went out.

examples.nl: Toen pas begreep ik de fout.
examples.en: Only then did I understand the error.

sections.title: 5. Tenses with toen
sections.body: The toen-clause is normally in the simple past. The main clause may be in the simple past too, or in the perfect when you talk about it as news ('Toen de telefoon ging, heb ik opgenomen'). If the main clause says something happened before the toen-moment, it uses the past perfect: 'was ... begonnen', 'had ... opgelost'. Auxiliaries follow the usual choice between hebben and zijn.

examples.nl: Toen ik aankwam, was de vergadering al begonnen.
examples.en: When I arrived, the meeting had already started.

examples.nl: Toen de monteur arriveerde, had ik het probleem al opgelost.
examples.en: When the technician arrived, I had already solved the problem.

examples.nl: Toen ik de fout ontdekte, ben ik naar mijn manager gelopen.
examples.en: When I discovered the error, I walked to my manager.

sections.title: 6. Toen versus als and wanneer
sections.body: For one occasion in the past Dutch uses toen. For repeated occasions in the past it uses als or wanneer, sometimes with words such as altijd or vroeger. The Flemish language advice treats toen as correct only for a single past occasion or period and recommends wanneer for repetition, while Dutch sources also accept als there. In Belgium, then, toen is the only correct conjunction for a single past event. A closed period still takes toen even when something happens regularly inside it.

examples.nl: Toen ik jong was, woonde ik in Gent.
examples.en: When I was young, I lived in Ghent.

examples.nl: Wanneer mijn vader thuiskwam, aten we altijd samen.
examples.en: Whenever my father came home, we always ate together.

examples.nl: Toen we klein waren, gingen we elke zomer naar zee.
examples.en: When we were small, we went to the sea every summer.

sections.title: 7. Modals, negation and questions
sections.body: A modal or a negation sits before the final verb of the toen-clause, as in 'Toen ik moest kiezen' and 'Toen ik niet reageerde'. The toen-clause itself usually stays in the simple past, while the main clause may use the perfect. A toen-clause can also follow a question word, and then the question keeps its own order.

examples.nl: Toen ik moest kiezen, nam ik de goedkoopste optie.
examples.en: When I had to choose, I took the cheapest option.

examples.nl: Toen ik niet reageerde, belde hij nog een keer.
examples.en: When I did not respond, he called once more.

examples.nl: Wat deed je toen de storing begon?
examples.en: What did you do when the outage began?

sections.title: 8. Not every toen is a conjunction
sections.body: Besides the conjunction and the adverb 'then', toen appears in fixed phrases such as 'toen pas' (only then) and 'toen al' (already then). They behave like the adverb: the verb is second. When you meet toen in a sentence, first decide which of the three uses it is by looking at where the finite verb stands.

examples.nl: Toen pas begreep ik de fout.
examples.en: Only then did I understand the error.

examples.nl: Toen kregen we eindelijk antwoord van de klant.
examples.en: Then we finally got an answer from the customer.

examples.nl: Toen het regende, zijn we in het café gebleven.
examples.en: When it rained, we stayed in the café.

mistakes.wrong: Toen ik kwam thuis, belde ik Zoë.
mistakes.right: Toen ik thuiskwam, belde ik Zoë.
mistakes.why: The separable verb is written together at the end of the toen-clause: thuiskwam.

mistakes.wrong: Toen ik thuiskwam, ik belde Zoë.
mistakes.right: Toen ik thuiskwam, belde ik Zoë.
mistakes.why: After a first dependent clause the main clause starts with its finite verb, so belde comes before ik.

mistakes.wrong: Toen ik vroeger vrij was, ging ik fietsen.
mistakes.right: Wanneer ik vroeger vrij was, ging ik fietsen.
mistakes.why: A repeated past habit is not one occasion, so wanneer or als is needed instead of toen.

mistakes.wrong: Toen ik belde mijn collega.
mistakes.right: Toen belde ik mijn collega.
mistakes.why: Toen as the adverb 'then' keeps the verb second; a verb-last order would turn it into an unfinished toen-clause.

mistakes.wrong: Toen ik aankwam, had de vergadering al begonnen.
mistakes.right: Toen ik aankwam, was de vergadering al begonnen.
mistakes.why: Beginnen forms its past perfect with zijn here, so the auxiliary is was.

sources: Toen of als of wanneer en verleden tijd — Taaladvies.net
Wanneer of als en tegenwoordige of toekomende tijd — Taaladvies.net

tot.title: Tot / totdat — until
tot.goal: Tell the preposition tot from the conjunctions tot and totdat, and put the verb in the right place when an event ends something.
tot.overview: Tot can be a preposition before a time or a place (tot vijf uur, tot aan de deur) and it can be a conjunction before a clause (tot de dokter me roept). Totdat is only a conjunction and always opens a clause. After a conjunction the finite verb goes to the end of its clause; after a preposition there is no verb at all. Tot also sits inside fixed combinations that have nothing to do with time (toegang tot, leiden tot).
tot.status: Detailed lesson, AI-edited. Not independently reviewed by a native speaker.

formulas.label: Conjunction after the main clause
formulas.pattern: Ik wacht | tot de dokter me roept.
formulas.why: The main clause keeps normal order; the tot-clause sends roept behind the object me.

formulas.label: Tot-clause first
formulas.pattern: Tot de dokter me roept, | blijf ik in de wachtkamer.
formulas.why: The whole tot-clause fills position one, so the main clause inverts to blijf ik.

formulas.label: Preposition with a time
formulas.pattern: Ik werk | tot vijf uur.
formulas.why: A clock time is no clause, so there is no second verb after tot.

formulas.label: Fixed combination
formulas.pattern: Ik heb toegang | tot de map.
formulas.why: Here tot belongs to the noun toegang and says nothing about time.

sections.title: 1. Is there a verb after it?
sections.body: Look at what follows tot. If a subject and a verb follow, tot is a conjunction and the verb moves to the end: 'Ik wacht tot de bus komt'. If only a time, a day or a place follows, tot is a preposition: 'Ik wacht tot twaalf uur'. The test is simply whether a second verb is needed.

examples.nl: Ik wacht tot de bus komt.
examples.en: I wait until the bus comes.

examples.nl: Ik wacht tot twaalf uur.
examples.en: I wait until twelve o'clock.

examples.nl: Tot nu toe is alles goed gegaan.
examples.en: Up to now everything has gone well.

sections.title: 2. Tot and totdat as conjunctions
sections.body: Before a clause, tot and totdat mean the same thing and both send the finite verb to the end. Totdat can only be a conjunction; tot can be both. In practice speakers use tot more often for short clauses and totdat when they want the clause to stand out. Neither changes the verb order.

examples.nl: Ik blijf proberen totdat het lukt.
examples.en: I keep trying until it works.

examples.nl: Zij wacht totdat de klant haar terugbelt.
examples.en: She waits until the customer calls her back.

examples.nl: Ik wacht tot mijn collega mij heeft teruggebeld.
examples.en: I wait until my colleague has called me back.

sections.title: 3. The clause can come first
sections.body: When the tot-clause opens the sentence, it fills position one and the main clause inverts. The verb of the tot-clause still goes last, and the main clause then starts with its own finite verb. So 'Tot de les begint, lees ik mijn notities' has two verbs in the wrong English position: begint at the end of clause one, lees at the start of clause two.

examples.nl: Tot de les begint, lees ik mijn notities.
examples.en: Until the lesson starts, I read my notes.

examples.nl: Totdat ik meer weet, zeg ik niets.
examples.en: Until I know more, I say nothing.

examples.nl: Tot ik antwoord heb, blijft het ticket open.
examples.en: Until I have an answer, the ticket stays open.

sections.title: 4. Verb groups at the end
sections.body: Perfect tenses, passives and separable verbs all end up behind the object inside the tot-clause. A separable verb is written together there: 'tot ik terugbel', not 'tot ik bel terug'. Participles come last: 'tot de vergadering is afgelopen'. The finite verb is the one that carries the person ending.

examples.nl: Wacht even tot ik terugbel.
examples.en: Wait a moment until I call back.

examples.nl: Ik blijf hier tot de vergadering is afgelopen.
examples.en: I stay here until the meeting is over.

examples.nl: Totdat de storing is verholpen, gebruiken we de reserveserver.
examples.en: Until the fault is fixed, we use the backup server.

sections.title: 5. The preposition tot
sections.body: As a preposition tot takes a noun phrase: a clock time, a day, a moment or a place. There is no verb to move. 'Tot' + 'aan' is a stronger limit and is often used for places. A noun can also hide an event: 'tot mijn terugkomst' says the same as 'tot ik terugkom', but with a noun and no extra clause.

examples.nl: De winkel is open tot negen uur.
examples.en: The shop is open until nine o'clock.

examples.nl: Van maandag tot vrijdag werk ik thuis.
examples.en: From Monday to Friday I work from home.

examples.nl: Het water stijgt tot aan de deur.
examples.en: The water rises up to the door.

sections.title: 6. Tot nu toe and other fixed phrases
sections.body: Some phrases are learned as a whole. 'Tot nu toe' means 'so far' and 'tot nu toe' fills a normal position in the sentence. 'Tot ziens' and 'tot morgen' are greetings. These phrases have no clause and no verb of their own; treat them as one adverb.

examples.nl: Wij hebben tot nu toe vijf meldingen ontvangen.
examples.en: We have received five reports so far.

examples.nl: Tot zondag heb ik vakantie.
examples.en: Until Sunday I am on holiday.

examples.nl: Het kan wachten tot volgende week.
examples.en: It can wait until next week.

sections.title: 7. Tot as a fixed preposition
sections.body: Many words take tot and have no time meaning at all. 'Toegang tot' is access to, 'leiden tot' is to lead to, 'zich wenden tot' is to turn to someone, 'promoveren tot' is to be promoted to. Learn each combination with its noun or verb; the preposition is not predictable from English alone.

examples.nl: Ik heb toegang tot de map.
examples.en: I have access to the folder.

examples.nl: Dat leidt tot problemen.
examples.en: That leads to problems.

examples.nl: Hij wendt zich tot de manager.
examples.en: He turns to the manager.

mistakes.wrong: Ik wacht totdat hij is klaar.
mistakes.right: Ik wacht totdat hij klaar is.
mistakes.why: In a dependent clause the finite verb goes to the end, so is follows the predicate klaar.

mistakes.wrong: Ik werk tot is vijf uur.
mistakes.right: Ik werk tot vijf uur.
mistakes.why: A clock time is not a clause. As a preposition tot needs no verb after it.

mistakes.wrong: Ik wacht tot mijn collega heeft mij teruggebeld.
mistakes.right: Ik wacht tot mijn collega mij heeft teruggebeld.
mistakes.why: Both parts of the perfect group go behind the object in the dependent clause, not before it.

mistakes.wrong: Tot de les begint, ik lees mijn notities.
mistakes.right: Tot de les begint, lees ik mijn notities.
mistakes.why: After a fronted clause the main clause starts with its finite verb: lees ik, not ik lees.

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb toegang aan de map.
mistakes.right: Ik heb toegang tot de map.
mistakes.why: The noun toegang takes tot; another preposition sounds wrong here and has to be learned with the noun.

verbs.title: Verbs in context — hebben, moeten, hoeven, proberen
verbs.goal: Choose the right verb and construct present, past, perfect and obligation sentences without translating 'have to' as hebben.
verbs.overview: Dutch uses hebben to possess something or as a perfect-tense auxiliary; moeten expresses 'have to/must'; hoeven in negative contexts means 'need to' and normally takes te + infinitive. The conjugated verb carries tense and person; other verbs keep their required infinitive or participle form.
verbs.status: Expanded teaching module (AI-edited, not independently reviewed by a native speaker); broader course and exercise review pending. Sections 7 to 10 (inseparable verbs, fixed prepositions, reflexive verbs, infinitive groups) were added with the 100 analysed cards and are AI-edited without external source checks.

formulas.label: Possession: hebben
formulas.pattern: Ik | heb | werk.
formulas.why: Heb means 'have'; werk is a noun, not an infinitive.

formulas.label: Necessity: moeten + infinitive
formulas.pattern: Ik | moet | werken.
formulas.why: English 'I have to work' is Dutch 'Ik moet werken', not 'Ik heb werken'.

formulas.label: No necessity: niet/geen/niets hoeven te
formulas.pattern: Ik | hoef | niets meer te doen.
formulas.why: Use hoef ... te + infinitive for 'I don't have to do anything anymore'.

formulas.label: Completed action: hebben + participle
formulas.pattern: Ik | heb | het werk gedaan.
formulas.why: Heb is now an auxiliary; gedaan is the past participle of doen.

formulas.label: Try to: proberen + te
formulas.pattern: Ik | probeer | Nederlands te spreken.
formulas.why: Proberen often combines with te + infinitive, not with a second finite verb.

sections.title: 1. Hebben means to have something
sections.body: If a noun follows, hebben can mean possession, ownership or a situation you experience. This is not the same as English 'have to + verb'.

examples.nl: Ik heb vandaag veel werk.
examples.en: I have a lot of work today.

examples.nl: Heb je morgen tijd?
examples.en: Do you have time tomorrow?

examples.nl: Ik heb een afspraak bij de tandarts.
examples.en: I have a dentist appointment.

sections.title: 2. Why 'I have to work' is MOETEN
sections.body: English uses have to for necessity. Dutch uses the modal moeten plus the bare infinitive. The modal itself changes with the subject: ik moet, jij moet, wij moeten.

examples.nl: Ik moet vandaag werken.
examples.en: I have to work today.

examples.nl: Zij moet het formulier invullen.
examples.en: She has to fill in the form.

examples.nl: Morgen moeten we vroeg vertrekken.
examples.en: Tomorrow we have to leave early.

sections.title: 3. Don't have to: hoeven + te + infinitive
sections.body: In negative or restrictive contexts, hoeven says that something is not necessary. 'Ik hoef niet te werken' is unambiguously 'I don't have to work'. 'Ik moet niet werken' is common in some contexts, but may suggest an instruction not to work; hoeven is the safer choice when you mean no obligation.

examples.nl: Ik hoef morgen niet te werken.
examples.en: I don't have to work tomorrow.

examples.nl: Als het document klaar is, hoef ik niets meer te doen.
examples.en: Once the document is ready, I don't need to do anything else.

examples.nl: Je hoeft vandaag geen afspraak te maken.
examples.en: You don't need to make an appointment today.

sections.title: 4. Hebben as an auxiliary in the perfect tense
sections.body: When hebben is followed by a past participle, it can build the perfect. Compare 'Ik doe het' (present) and 'Ik heb het gedaan' (completed). Some other verbs form their perfect with zijn, not hebben.

examples.nl: Ik doe de afwas.
examples.en: I'm doing the dishes.

examples.nl: Ik heb de afwas gedaan.
examples.en: I've done the dishes.

examples.nl: Ik ben naar huis gegaan.
examples.en: I went home / I've gone home.

sections.title: 5. Proberen, and why te stays
sections.body: Proberen often takes 'te + infinitive' for trying to do an action. A modal such as moeten normally takes a bare infinitive instead. Don't use two conjugated verbs next to each other in a simple main clause.

examples.nl: Ik probeer Nederlands te spreken.
examples.en: I'm trying to speak Dutch.

examples.nl: Gisteren probeerde ik je te bellen.
examples.en: Yesterday I tried to call you.

examples.nl: Ik heb geprobeerd het probleem op te lossen.
examples.en: I've tried to solve the problem.

sections.title: 6. Choose the meaning before the word order
sections.body: Ask yourself: possession (hebben + noun), necessity (moeten + infinitive), no necessity (hoeven + te), completed action (auxiliary + participle), or intention/attempt (proberen + te)? Then put the conjugated verb in main-clause V2.

examples.nl: Ik heb werk, maar ik hoef nu niets te doen.
examples.en: I have work, but I don't need to do anything now.

examples.nl: Als ik morgen moet werken, sta ik vroeg op.
examples.en: If I have to work tomorrow, I get up early.

examples.nl: Ik weet dat ik het nog moet doen.
examples.en: I know that I still have to do it.

sections.title: 7. Inseparable verbs never split
sections.body: Verbs that start with an unstressed prefix such as be-, ver-, ont- and her- are inseparable: bezoeken, begrijpen, verkopen, ontdekken, herhalen. The finite form stays whole ('Ik bezoek mijn grootmoeder'), the participle has no ge- ('bezocht', 'begrepen') and nothing is left at the end of the clause. Compare the separable 'opbellen': 'Ik bel mijn grootmoeder op'.

examples.nl: Ik bezoek mijn grootmoeder.
examples.en: I visit my grandmother.

examples.nl: Zij begrijpt de opdracht niet.
examples.en: She does not understand the assignment.

examples.nl: Wij verkopen onze oude fiets.
examples.en: We are selling our old bike.

sections.title: 8. Verbs with a fixed preposition
sections.body: Many verbs come with a preposition that you must learn together: wachten op, denken aan, houden van, luisteren naar, kijken naar, praten over, zorgen voor, beginnen met, lachen om. The English preposition is no guide: 'wait for' is 'wachten op', 'listen to' is 'luisteren naar'. Some verbs change meaning with the preposition: denken aan (have in mind) versus denken over (have an opinion).

examples.nl: Ik wacht op de bus.
examples.en: I am waiting for the bus.

examples.nl: Zij houdt van muziek.
examples.en: She loves music.

examples.nl: Wij praten over het project.
examples.en: We are talking about the project.

sections.title: 9. Reflexive verbs
sections.body: A reflexive verb is used with a pronoun that refers back to the subject: ik herinner me, hij vergist zich, wij haasten ons, ik voel me. The pronoun follows the finite verb in a main clause. English often has no pronoun for the same idea, so a reflexive pronoun is easy to forget.

examples.nl: Ik herinner me die dag.
examples.en: I remember that day.

examples.nl: Hij vergist zich in het adres.
examples.en: He is mistaken about the address.

examples.nl: Ik voel me vandaag goed.
examples.en: I feel well today.

sections.title: 10. Verbs that take an infinitive
sections.body: Some verbs take a bare infinitive (modals, laten, blijven, gaan, komen): 'Ik laat het je zien', 'Hij blijft werken', 'Ik ga koken'. Others take te (proberen, besluiten, durven, weigeren, beloven, hopen) or 'om te' after a noun or an adjective. Learn which pattern each verb follows. Hoeven needs niet and te: 'Ik hoef niet te werken'.

examples.nl: Ik ga koken voor mijn vrienden.
examples.en: I am going to cook for my friends.

examples.nl: Ik probeer vroeg te slapen.
examples.en: I try to sleep early.

examples.nl: Het is moeilijk om een keuze te maken.
examples.en: It is difficult to make a choice.

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb niets doen.
mistakes.right: Ik hoef niets te doen.
mistakes.why: To say 'I don't have to do anything', use hoeven with te + infinitive. 'Heb ... gedaan' would mean 'have done', a different time and meaning.

mistakes.wrong: Morgen heb ik werken.
mistakes.right: Morgen moet ik werken.
mistakes.why: English 'have to work' uses the Dutch modal moeten, not possession verb hebben.

mistakes.wrong: Ik ben probeer Nederlands.
mistakes.right: Ik probeer Nederlands te spreken.
mistakes.why: Probeer is already the finite present verb; don't add ben before it. Add a complete infinitive phrase for what you are trying to do.

mistakes.wrong: Ik zoek mijn grootmoeder be.
mistakes.right: Ik bezoek mijn grootmoeder.
mistakes.why: Bezoeken is inseparable because of the unstressed prefix be-; its finite form never splits and no particle can be left at the end of the clause.

mistakes.wrong: Ik wacht voor de bus.
mistakes.right: Ik wacht op de bus.
mistakes.why: The verb wachten takes the preposition op, not voor; the English 'wait for' is no guide to the Dutch preposition.

mistakes.wrong: Ik herinner die dag.
mistakes.right: Ik herinner me die dag.
mistakes.why: Zich herinneren is a reflexive verb and needs the pronoun me after the finite verb; without it the sentence is incomplete.

sources: Hoeven versus moeten — Team Taaladvies Vlaanderen

tense.title: Past and perfect — verleden tijd en voltooid tegenwoordige tijd
tense.goal: Choose between simple past and perfect, pick hebben or zijn, form the participle correctly, and place the verbs in main clauses, dependent clauses and questions.
tense.overview: Dutch tells the past with two tenses. The simple past (ik werkte) narrates and describes; the perfect (ik heb gewerkt) reports a finished event and links it to now, and in speech it is the usual way to say that something happened. The perfect is built from an auxiliary (hebben or zijn) in the verb-second slot and a participle at the end, so the choice of auxiliary and the form of the participle are the two things to learn.
tense.status: Detailed lesson, AI-edited and aligned with the 100 analysed Past & perfect cards. The rules for 't kofschip, ge- and the choice of hebben or zijn are standard but have not been checked against an external source for this lesson; the statements about spoken preference are stated cautiously. No native-speaker review.

formulas.label: Present
formulas.pattern: Ik | werk | thuis.
formulas.why: One finite verb in slot two.

formulas.label: Simple past
formulas.pattern: Ik | werkte | thuis.
formulas.why: Weak verbs add -te or -de, strong verbs change the stem vowel: werkte, nam, ging.

formulas.label: Perfect
formulas.pattern: Ik | heb | thuis | gewerkt.
formulas.why: The auxiliary takes slot two and the participle goes to the end of the clause.

formulas.label: Perfect with zijn
formulas.pattern: Ik | ben | gisteren naar Gent | gegaan.
formulas.why: Verbs of movement and change of state use zijn: ben gegaan, is vertrokken, is geworden.

formulas.label: Perfect in a dependent clause
formulas.pattern: ... dat hij het verslag | heeft gelezen.
formulas.why: The verb group goes to the end of the dependent clause, the finite auxiliary first.

formulas.label: Past perfect
formulas.pattern: Ik | had | het rapport al | gelezen.
formulas.why: The auxiliary is in the simple past: had or was.

sections.title: 1. Simple past or perfect?
sections.body: Use the simple past to narrate a story and to describe how things were: 'Gisteren ging alles goed', 'Het was druk'. Use the perfect to report that something has happened and matters now, or to speak about a period that is not over: 'Ik heb deze week elke dag gefietst'. In everyday speech the perfect is the usual choice for a finished event, so do not treat it as a second-class tense.

examples.nl: Gisteren ging alles goed.
examples.en: Yesterday everything went well.

examples.nl: Vanochtend heb ik drie vergaderingen gehad.
examples.en: This morning I have had three meetings.

examples.nl: Ik heb deze week elke dag gefietst.
examples.en: I have cycled every day this week.

sections.title: 2. The simple past of weak verbs
sections.body: Weak verbs add -de or -te to the stem, and the plural adds -n: werkte, werkten; speelde, speelden. The choice depends on the last sound of the stem: after one of t, k, f, s, ch, p (the 't kofschip sounds) the ending is -te, otherwise -de. The participle follows the same rule: gewerkt, gespeeld.

examples.nl: Zij werkte tot vijf uur.
examples.en: She worked until five.

examples.nl: Hij speelde elke zaterdag voetbal.
examples.en: He played football every Saturday.

examples.nl: We wachtten een uur op de bus.
examples.en: We waited an hour for the bus.

sections.title: 3. Strong and irregular verbs
sections.body: Strong verbs change their stem vowel and have no ending in the singular: zag, nam, schreef, vond, sprak. The plural often has a different vowel length: zagen, namen, schreven. Some verbs are irregular in other ways: gaan (ging), zijn (was), kopen (kocht). The participle usually ends in -en: gezien, genomen, geschreven. Learn the three forms of each strong verb together.

examples.nl: Ik zag haar gisteren in de stad.
examples.en: I saw her in town yesterday.

examples.nl: Hij nam de eerste trein.
examples.en: He took the first train.

examples.nl: We reden langs de kust.
examples.en: We drove along the coast.

sections.title: 4. Hebben or zijn?
sections.body: Most verbs form the perfect with hebben, especially verbs with a direct object (lezen, kopen) and activities (werken, praten). Verbs that express movement from one place to another or a change of state take zijn: gaan, komen, vertrekken, verhuizen, worden, bevriezen, stijgen. Blijven and zijn also take zijn. Some verbs depend on meaning: lopen or rijden to a destination take zijn, as an activity hebben is also possible. In Flanders position verbs such as zitten and staan are also heard with zijn.

examples.nl: Ik heb het rapport gelezen.
examples.en: I have read the report.

examples.nl: Ik ben gisteren naar de markt gegaan.
examples.en: I went to the market yesterday.

examples.nl: Het ijs is gesmolten.
examples.en: The ice has melted.

sections.title: 5. The participle and ge-
sections.body: The regular participle is ge- + stem + -d or -t: gewerkt, gebeld. Verbs that begin with an unstressed prefix get no ge-: be-, ge-, her-, ont-, ver-. So betaald, ontdekt, verkocht, herkend. Separable verbs put ge- between the particle and the stem: opgestuurd, aangekomen, uitgevallen. But a separable verb whose stem begins with an unstressed prefix gets none: voorbereid. Strong participles end in -en.

examples.nl: Wij hebben de bestelling betaald.
examples.en: We have paid for the order.

examples.nl: Hij heeft de fout ontdekt.
examples.en: He has discovered the error.

examples.nl: Zij heeft de lessen voorbereid.
examples.en: She has prepared the lessons.

sections.title: 6. The perfect with a modal
sections.body: With a modal verb the perfect does not use a participle of the modal. Instead there are two infinitives at the end: 'Ik heb moeten werken', 'Zij heeft niet kunnen komen'. The auxiliary is hebben. With 'gaan' plus infinitive the auxiliary is zijn: 'Ik ben gaan wandelen'.

examples.nl: Ik heb gisteren moeten werken.
examples.en: I had to work yesterday.

examples.nl: Zij heeft niet kunnen komen.
examples.en: She could not come.

examples.nl: Ik ben vanmiddag even gaan wandelen.
examples.en: I went for a short walk this afternoon.

sections.title: 7. Dependent clauses and questions
sections.body: In a dependent clause the verb group goes to the end, with the finite auxiliary first: 'dat hij het verslag heeft gelezen', 'dat zij al is vertrokken'. In a yes/no question the auxiliary opens the sentence and the participle stays at the end: 'Heb je de brief geschreven?'. With a question word the auxiliary is second: 'Wat heb je gisteren gedaan?'. With 'je' after the verb the -t of 'hebt' and 'bent' falls away.

examples.nl: Ik weet dat hij het verslag heeft gelezen.
examples.en: I know that he has read the report.

examples.nl: Heb je de brief geschreven?
examples.en: Have you written the letter?

examples.nl: Waarom ben je zo laat gekomen?
examples.en: Why did you come so late?

sections.title: 8. The past perfect
sections.body: The past perfect puts an event before another moment in the past. It is the perfect with the auxiliary in the simple past: had gelezen, was vertrokken. 'Al' (already) and 'nog niet' (not yet) often accompany it. A state such as 'weg zijn' needs no participle: 'De trein was al weg'.

examples.nl: Ik had het rapport al gelezen.
examples.en: I had already read the report.

examples.nl: Zij was al vertrokken.
examples.en: She had already left.

examples.nl: Hij had de brief nog niet gestuurd.
examples.en: He had not yet sent the letter.

sections.title: 9. Putting it together
sections.body: For any past sentence ask four questions: is it narration or a report; which auxiliary does the verb need; what is the participle; and which clause am I in. The answers decide the word order. 'Vorige week heb ik mijn tante gebeld' has a fronted time phrase, so the auxiliary comes before the subject. 'Omdat het gisteren heeft geregend, bleef ik thuis' has a dependent clause with the verb group at its end and a simple past in the main clause.

examples.nl: Vorige week heb ik mijn tante gebeld.
examples.en: Last week I phoned my aunt.

examples.nl: Omdat het gisteren heeft geregend, bleef ik thuis.
examples.en: Because it rained yesterday, I stayed at home.

examples.nl: Ik heb de e-mail beantwoord.
examples.en: I have answered the email.

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb gewerk.
mistakes.right: Ik heb gewerkt.
mistakes.why: The participle of werken ends in -t after the stem sound k.

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb gisteren naar de markt gegaan.
mistakes.right: Ik ben gisteren naar de markt gegaan.
mistakes.why: Gaan is a verb of movement and takes zijn, not hebben.

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb de fout geontdekt.
mistakes.right: Ik heb de fout ontdekt.
mistakes.why: Ontdekken begins with the unstressed prefix ont-, so the participle has no ge-.

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb gisteren gemoeten werken.
mistakes.right: Ik heb gisteren moeten werken.
mistakes.why: With a modal the perfect uses the infinitive, not a participle: heb ... moeten werken.

mistakes.wrong: Ik weet dat hij heeft het verslag gelezen.
mistakes.right: Ik weet dat hij het verslag heeft gelezen.
mistakes.why: In a dependent clause the verb group goes to the end, behind the object.

wanneer.title: WANNEER — time clause, direct question, indirect question
wanneer.goal: Recognise the three jobs of wanneer and put the finite verb in the right place for each of them.
wanneer.overview: Wanneer does three jobs. It can open a time clause (when, whenever), it can be the question word of a direct question, and it can introduce an indirect question. Each job has its own word order: the time clause and the indirect question send the verb to the end, the direct question puts the verb right behind wanneer. For a single past occasion Dutch uses toen, not wanneer.
wanneer.status: Detailed lesson, AI-edited. The statements on wanneer versus als, on register, and on repeated versus single past occasions were checked against Taaladvies pages on 27 October 2026 (see sources). Everything else is not independently reviewed by a native speaker.

formulas.label: Time clause after the main clause
formulas.pattern: Ik bel je | wanneer ik thuis ben.
formulas.why: The main clause keeps normal order and the wanneer-clause ends with ben.

formulas.label: Time clause first
formulas.pattern: Wanneer ik thuis ben, | bel ik je.
formulas.why: The whole wanneer-clause fills position one, so the main clause inverts to bel ik.

formulas.label: Direct question
formulas.pattern: Wanneer | vertrekt | de bus?
formulas.why: The finite verb vertrekt follows the question word immediately and the subject comes after it.

formulas.label: Indirect question
formulas.pattern: Ik weet niet | wanneer de bus vertrekt.
formulas.why: Inside the embedded question the subject comes first and vertrekt moves to the end.

sections.title: 1. Three jobs, three word orders
sections.body: Look at where the finite verb stands. In 'Wanneer vertrekt de bus?' it follows wanneer. In 'Ik weet niet wanneer de bus vertrekt' it has moved to the end. In 'Wanneer de bus vertrekt, stappen we in' the wanneer-clause also ends in its verb and the main clause inverts. The same word asks, embeds and connects.

examples.nl: Wanneer vertrekt de bus?
examples.en: When does the bus depart?

examples.nl: Ik weet niet wanneer de bus vertrekt.
examples.en: I don't know when the bus leaves.

examples.nl: Wanneer de trein aankomt, stappen we in.
examples.en: When the train arrives, we board.

sections.title: 2. The wanneer time clause
sections.body: As a conjunction wanneer means 'when' for the present or the future, or 'whenever' for repetition. The clause is dependent, so the finite verb goes to the end, and a separable verb is written together there. In everyday Dutch als does the same job, and wanneer is the somewhat more formal choice.

examples.nl: Ik laat het je weten wanneer de back-up klaar is.
examples.en: I'll let you know when the backup is ready.

examples.nl: De les begint wanneer de docent binnenkomt.
examples.en: The lesson begins when the teacher comes in.

examples.nl: Wanneer je het formulier invult, krijg je een bevestiging.
examples.en: When you fill in the form, you get a confirmation.

sections.title: 3. Time clause first: inversion
sections.body: When the wanneer-clause opens the sentence it is one constituent, so the main clause starts with its finite verb and the subject follows. A separable verb in the main clause splits: 'bel ik je terug'. If the main clause comes first, nothing changes in it.

examples.nl: Wanneer ik de resultaten heb, bel ik je terug.
examples.en: When I have the results, I'll call you back.

examples.nl: Ik bel je terug wanneer ik de resultaten heb.
examples.en: I'll call you back when I have the results.

examples.nl: Wanneer het donker wordt, gaan de lampen automatisch aan.
examples.en: When it gets dark, the lights switch on automatically.

sections.title: 4. Direct questions
sections.body: A direct question is one main clause: wanneer, then the finite verb, then the subject. Modals and perfects follow the usual rules: only the finite part sits behind wanneer, and the infinitive or participle goes to the end. There is no auxiliary like English 'does'.

examples.nl: Wanneer begint je nieuwe baan?
examples.en: When does your new job start?

examples.nl: Wanneer kunnen we de wijziging testen?
examples.en: When can we test the change?

examples.nl: Wanneer heb je het ticket gesloten?
examples.en: When did you close the ticket?

sections.title: 5. Indirect questions
sections.body: After verbs of knowing, asking or telling, wanneer introduces an embedded question. It then behaves like any dependent clause: subject first, verb last. The direct question 'Wanneer komt de trein aan?' becomes 'Ik weet niet wanneer de trein aankomt'. Polite frames such as 'Kunt u mij zeggen' work the same way.

examples.nl: Kunt u mij zeggen wanneer het loket opengaat?
examples.en: Can you tell me when the counter opens?

examples.nl: Ik vraag me af wanneer de bestelling bezorgd wordt.
examples.en: I wonder when the order will be delivered.

examples.nl: Hij vroeg wanneer wij de fout hadden ontdekt.
examples.en: He asked when we had discovered the error.

sections.title: 6. Wanneer, als and toen
sections.body: For the present and the future wanneer and als are usually interchangeable, with wanneer more formal; only wanneer can ask a question. For repeated occasions in the past the Flemish language advice recommends wanneer, and Dutch sources also accept als. For one occasion in the past you must use toen, not wanneer. In Belgium toen is the only correct conjunction for a single past event.

examples.nl: Wanneer ik vroeger vrij was, ging ik fietsen.
examples.en: Whenever I was free in the past, I went cycling.

examples.nl: Toen ik aankwam, was de winkel dicht.
examples.en: When I arrived, the shop was closed.

examples.nl: Wanneer de klant belde, nam ik altijd meteen op.
examples.en: Whenever the customer called, I always picked up immediately.

sections.title: 7. Longer verb groups inside the clause
sections.body: Inside a wanneer-clause or an embedded question the finite verb is not always the last word. With a modal the finite verb comes before the infinitive, and with a perfect the auxiliary comes before the participle, but the group still closes the clause. Separable infinitives after a modal are not split.

examples.nl: Wanneer je het formulier hebt ingevuld, kun je betalen.
examples.en: When you have filled in the form, you can pay.

examples.nl: Ik zou graag willen weten wanneer de resultaten komen.
examples.en: I would like to know when the results will come.

examples.nl: Kunt u uitleggen wanneer ik de wijziging moet melden?
examples.en: Can you explain when I have to report the change?

sections.title: 8. Pas wanneer and fixed endings
sections.body: With pas ('only') the condition must be met first: 'Ik ga pas weg wanneer alle klanten zijn geholpen'. 'Wanneer je wilt' and 'wanneer het zover is' are fixed endings meaning 'whenever you like' and 'when the moment comes'. They are dependent clauses with the finite verb last.

examples.nl: Ik ga pas weg wanneer alle klanten zijn geholpen.
examples.en: I'll only leave when all customers have been helped.

examples.nl: Je kunt het wijzigen wanneer je wilt.
examples.en: You can change it whenever you want.

examples.nl: Hij zal het weten wanneer het zover is.
examples.en: He will know when the time comes.

mistakes.wrong: Ik weet niet wanneer begint de bus.
mistakes.right: Ik weet niet wanneer de bus vertrekt.
mistakes.why: An indirect question uses dependent order: the subject comes before the verb and the verb goes last.

mistakes.wrong: Wanneer de bus vertrekt?
mistakes.right: Wanneer vertrekt de bus?
mistakes.why: A direct question puts the finite verb right after wanneer, before the subject.

mistakes.wrong: Wanneer ik thuis ben, ik bel je.
mistakes.right: Wanneer ik thuis ben, bel ik je.
mistakes.why: After a first dependent clause the main clause starts with its finite verb.

mistakes.wrong: Wanneer ik aankwam, was de winkel dicht.
mistakes.right: Toen ik aankwam, was de winkel dicht.
mistakes.why: One occasion in the past needs toen, not wanneer.

mistakes.wrong: Ik zou graag willen weten wanneer komen de resultaten.
mistakes.right: Ik zou graag willen weten wanneer de resultaten komen.
mistakes.why: Inside the embedded question the verb moves to the end after the subject.

sources: Toen of als of wanneer en verleden tijd — Taaladvies.net
Wanneer of als en tegenwoordige of toekomende tijd — Taaladvies.net

terwijl.title: Terwijl — while, whereas, even though
terwijl.goal: Use terwijl for things that happen at the same time and for contrasts, and keep the verb order right in both clauses.
terwijl.overview: Terwijl is a subordinating conjunction. Its first and most common job is to say that two things happen at the same time. It can also contrast two situations (whereas) or name a surprising fact (even though). In every job the verb of the terwijl-clause goes to the end, and a terwijl-clause in first position makes the main clause invert. Tijdens (during) is a preposition and intussen or ondertussen (meanwhile) are adverbs; neither sends a verb to the end.
terwijl.status: Detailed lesson, AI-edited. Not independently reviewed by a native speaker.

formulas.label: Parallel action after the main clause
formulas.pattern: Ik kook | terwijl mijn broer de tafel dekt.
formulas.why: The main clause keeps normal order; the terwijl-clause sends dekt behind the object.

formulas.label: Terwijl-clause first
formulas.pattern: Terwijl ik studeer, | luistert Zoë naar muziek.
formulas.why: The whole terwijl-clause fills position one, so the main clause inverts to luistert Zoë.

formulas.label: Contrast
formulas.pattern: Mijn zus houdt van koffie, | terwijl ik liever thee drink.
formulas.why: After a comma terwijl sets two situations against each other; the verb is still last.

formulas.label: Preposition or adverb instead
formulas.pattern: Tijdens de les | schrijft hij aantekeningen.
formulas.why: Tijdens takes a noun and no second verb, so the sentence is one main clause.

sections.title: 1. Two things at the same time
sections.body: Terwijl joins two actions that run side by side. Each action keeps its own subject and verb: 'Ik kook terwijl mijn broer de tafel dekt'. The main clause says what the speaker is doing; the terwijl-clause adds the parallel action and ends with its verb. The same subject may return: 'We praten terwijl we lopen'.

examples.nl: Zij leest een boek terwijl de baby slaapt.
examples.en: She reads a book while the baby sleeps.

examples.nl: Hij belt zijn moeder terwijl hij op de bus wacht.
examples.en: He calls his mother while he waits for the bus.

examples.nl: We praten terwijl we naar het station lopen.
examples.en: We talk while we walk to the station.

sections.title: 2. The terwijl-clause first
sections.body: When the terwijl-clause opens the sentence it fills position one, so the main clause starts with its finite verb: 'Terwijl ik studeer, luistert Zoë'. The verb of the first clause is last, and the verb of the second clause comes straight after the comma. Count the verbs: one at the end of clause one, one at the start of clause two.

examples.nl: Terwijl de pasta kookt, snijd ik de groenten.
examples.en: While the pasta cooks, I cut the vegetables.

examples.nl: Terwijl wij eten, vertelt Daan over zijn reis.
examples.en: While we eat, Daan tells about his trip.

examples.nl: Terwijl de printer afdrukt, beantwoord ik mijn e-mails.
examples.en: While the printer prints, I answer my e-mails.

sections.title: 3. Verb groups inside the clause
sections.body: Perfects, passives and modals end the terwijl-clause as a group. A separable verb is written together: 'terwijl jij de afwas afdroogt'. After 'beginnen' the clause ends in 'te' plus infinitive: 'terwijl het begint te regenen'. In the main clause the same separable verbs split: 'ik ruim de kamer op'.

examples.nl: Ik ruim de kamer op terwijl jij de afwas afdroogt.
examples.en: I tidy the room while you dry the dishes.
